passage: Welcome to our FAQ on the Vedic Period. Many students ask about the social structure of this time. The Varna system was not always rigid; in the early Vedic period, status was often based on one's work or skills rather than just being determined by birth. Regarding the Rigveda, it is a common mistake to think only men composed its hymns; in fact, several women sages also composed these sacred verses. When we look at political life, the Raja did not have absolute power. He had to consult the Sabha and Samiti, which were assemblies where people discussed matters and made decisions together, rather than the king acting alone. We also find evidence of social differences in burials. For example, when archaeologists find gold beads in a grave, it indicates the status of the person buried there, as these items were valuable markers of wealth and rank. Finally, regarding the people known as the Dasas, they were not simply people who could not speak. They were a distinct group of people who did not perform sacrifices and spoke a different language, which is why they were often described as 'non-sacrificers' rather than just being silent.

items.evidence: The Varna system was not always rigid; in the early Vedic period, status was often based on one's work or skills rather than just being determined by birth.
items.q: In the early Vedic period, a skilled potter's son became a respected poet. How is this explained?
options: Status often depended on skills, not only birth
Status was fixed at birth but rules were ignored
Only priests could ever change their status
Status came from the gold a family owned
items.explain: In the early Vedic period, status was often based on work or skills, not just birth.

wrong.why: thinks varna was always fixed by birth
thinks only priests had special rights
links status only to wealth from burials

items.evidence: Regarding the Rigveda, it is a common mistake to think only men composed its hymns; in fact, several women sages also composed these sacred verses.
items.q: A student says a Rigveda hymn must have a male author. Why is this claim weak?
options: Some hymns were composed by women sages
Hymns were composed by kings, not sages
Hymns were written by later scribes in books
Hymns were sung only by the Dasas
items.explain: Several women sages also composed Rigvedic hymns, so authorship was not only male.

wrong.why: thinks only men composed hymns, so shifts to kings
thinks the Rigveda was written in books
picks a group named elsewhere in the passage

items.evidence: He had to consult the Sabha and Samiti, which were assemblies where people discussed matters and made decisions together, rather than the king acting alone.
items.q: A Raja wants to start a war. What would he most likely have to do first?
options: Talk it over with the people's assemblies
Order his tax officers to decide for him
Wait for the priests to build him a palace
Ask the Dasas to approve his plan
items.explain: The Raja had to consult the Sabha and Samiti, where decisions were made together.

wrong.why: thinks the king alone decided through his officers
thinks rajas had palaces and tax systems
mixes up the Dasas with the assemblies

items.evidence: They were a distinct group of people who did not perform sacrifices and spoke a different language, which is why they were often described as 'non-sacrificers' rather than just being silent.
items.q: Why were the Dasas often called 'non-sacrificers'?
options: They followed different practices and spoke another tongue
They were silent and had no language
They were forbidden to join any assembly
They fought wars only to capture land
items.explain: Dasas were a distinct group who did not perform sacrifices and spoke a different language.

wrong.why: thinks Dasas simply could not speak
mixes sacrifice rules with exclusion from rites
links Dasas to wars for land
